title: A surprising superbubble
caption: The superbubble in the star-forming region N44, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope, Chandra and Spitzer
celestial: LHA 120-N 44, NGC 1929 · constellation Dorado · about 150000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: Optical: ESO, X-ray: NASA/CXC/U.Mich./S.Oey, IR: NASA/JPL

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Blue, red and yellow blend in this view of the star-forming region LHA 120-N44 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the Milky Way's small companion galaxies. At its heart lies the star cluster NGC 1929.

The massive stars in that cluster give off intense radiation, blow matter out at high speed as stellar winds, and live fast before exploding as supernovae. Together, the winds and supernova shock waves have hollowed out a huge cavity in the surrounding gas, called a superbubble.

Each color shows a different kind of light. X-rays from NASA's Chandra, shown in blue, trace very hot gas. Infrared from NASA's Spitzer, in red, shows dust and cooler gas, and the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope's visible-light view, in yellow, shows the young stars and glowing clouds. Together they helped explain why N44 is so bright in X-rays. Supernova shocks hit the cavity walls, and hot material evaporates from them.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (25.28 x 20.18 arcminutes) and distance (150000 light years), the frame spans roughly 1,100 × 881 light-years. Its light set out about 150,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This multi-telescope composite shows Chandra X-ray data in blue, Spitzer infrared data in red, and visible light from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope in yellow.
understand.eye: X-rays and infrared light are both invisible to the human eye. Only the yellow part of this image shows light we could see.

explore: The name LHA 120-N44 comes from a 1956 catalog, put together by the American astronomer and astronaut Karl Henize, listing stars and nebulae in the Magellanic Clouds that shine in hydrogen-alpha light. The letter N marks it as a nebula, and it is often called simply N44.
